subject: PrivDeploy: sustained-burst sizing & egress budget — PolarisHealth
messages:
From: Alex Durand <alex.durand@polarishealth.com>
To: rishi_malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 14 Sep 2026 08:22:00 -0700
Subject: Private deployment questions — sustained bursts and egress caps

Rishi,

Quick context: PolarisHealth is moving inference for our triage and summarization flows into a VPC private deployment. Our real concern is the 10–20 minute sustained-burst windows during business hours (clinician review sessions). We need guidance on sizing a private GPU pool so we can commit a procurement SKU and set expectations with infra.

Key constraints:
- Typical request: ~1–2k tokens input, ~600–1,500 tokens output (model: policy-guided summarizer).
- SLO: 95th pct latency < 300ms for the short-form endpoint; availability target 99.5% for business hours.
- On-prem egress policy: max egress to public internet 4 Gbps (hard cap) and single NIC 25 Gbps on our host.
- Want a plan that keeps critical traffic local and can fail-over to Redwood hosted API if capacity is exhausted.

Questions:
1) Given the above, what minimum GPU pool (count + flavor) should we reserve to hit the SLO for a 20-minute sustained burst of 60k tokens/sec aggregate?
2) What NIC/egress headroom should we plan for (including prefix cache/pop-warm traffic and model checkpoint pullback)?
3) Operational guidance: warm pools, admission-control thresholds, and runbook items to avoid a full outage if we hit the egress cap.

Appreciate an initial sizing + ops checklist we can share with our networking and procurement teams. Happy to jump on a quick call.

— Alex
Alex Durand
Head of Platform Engineering, PolarisHealth
From: rishi_malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.com>
To: Alex Durand <alex.durand@polarishealth.com>
Cc: laura_bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 14 Sep 2026 12:30:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Private deployment questions — sustained bursts and egress caps

Alex — thanks for the clear constraints. Below is an initial, conservative plan and a short list of follow-ups. I copied Laura (Customer Success / capacity) for commercial sizing and Markus (Infra PM) for NIC/ops specifics.

Summary (short):
- Baseline recommendation: provision a 6-GPU private pool (4 active compute + 2 warm standbys) of A100-equivalent instances. This gives ~2.5x headroom vs your 60k tokens/sec sustained-burst assumption under our benchmarked model variant (redwood-summarize-large-int8).
- NIC & egress: dual 25 Gbps NICs (bonded) recommended; plan for 500 Mbps sustained egress per 1k sustained RPS in worst-case output-size scenarios.
- Operational controls: soft admission control at 70% pool utilization, hard throttle and graceful fallback to hosted API at 90% utilization; prefix/KV cache warm on cold start; warm pool warmup to handle short spikes.

Need to confirm a few specifics to tighten the numbers:
- exact average output token size during your peak windows (you listed 600–1,500 — can you share sample histograms?)
- acceptable fraction of traffic that may be failovered to hosted (we'll model cost + latency hit)

I'll follow up with a short internal calc and the workbook attached.

Cheers,
Rishi
Head of Sales Engineering
Redwood Inference
From: rishi_malhotra <rishi_malhotma@redwood.com>
To: laura_bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.com>, markus_klein <markus_klein@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 15 Sep 2026 09:10:00 -07:00
Subject: FW: Private deployment questions — sustained bursts and egress caps

Laura / Markus — forwarding PolarisHealth's ask. Below are the quick capacity math notes I used and the ops play we should propose back. Please sanity-check and add any procurement language (commit SKUs / warm capacity) we should include.

Assumptions we used:
- Target sustained-burst: 60,000 tokens/sec aggregate (customer-provided scenario).
- Reference perf: redwood-summarize-large-int8 @ 512 context -> effective steady-state throughput = ~12,000 tokens/sec per GPU under continuous batched streaming with our optimized kernels and KV prefix caching. (This is a lab number; variance ±20% in field.)
- Safety factors: +25% for model perf variance, +25% for headroom = combined factor ~1.56.

Sizing calc (rounding up):
- Required raw GPUs = 60,000 / 12,000 = 5.0 GPUs.
- With safety factor 1.56 -> 5.0 * 1.56 = 7.8 -> round to 8 GPUs.
- Operational split: 5 GPUs active compute, 2 GPUs reserved for warm pre-warmed cache/warm pool, 1 GPU as spare for failover/maintenance -> total 8.

NIC / egress notes: estimate egress per token (response payload + protocol overhead) = ~0.08 KB/token for text-only summarization (conservative).
- At 60,000 tokens/sec -> 60k * 0.08KB = 4,800 KB/s = ~38.4 Mbps sustained outbound for model responses.
- Add control / checkpoint pulls / periodic model diffs and warmup chatter -> plan for 5x multiplier during ramp windows -> ~192 Mbps.
- Recommendation: 2 x 25 Gbps NICs is over-provisioning but provides margin for other services; we should at minimum ensure the VPC egress policy allows transient ramps up to 1 Gbps for warmup windows.

Autoscale & admission-control policy (ops):
- Warm pool: keep 25% of total capacity warm (in this plan, 2 GPUs) with KV cache pre-warmed. Warm pool should be kept 'hot' for 10 minutes windows using light health-check traffic.
- Soft admission control: when active compute GPUs reach 70% average utilization over a 60s window, start throttling low-priority requests and route them to hosted API.
- Hard failover: at 90% utilization persist for 2 minutes -> trigger immediate spillover to hosted API for configured tenants; notify on-call and open incident.
- Queueing thresholds: if median queue time > 150ms or P95 queue > 400ms, start aggressive request shedding for non-critical endpoints.

Runbook highlights (short):
- Pre-burst checklist (30 min before expected window): ensure warm pool at 100%, prefetch prefix cache, verify health of cross-host NVLink and NIC bonding, check BGP/route priority for hosted fallback.
- During burst: monitor token/sec, GPU util, queue depth, NIC throughput; if we hit soft admission control, apply traffic shaping rules in order: background jobs -> bulk-batch requests -> low-priority summarizers.
- Post-burst: drain warm pool to baseline over 20 minutes to avoid oscillation.

Edge cases to call out:
- If output token sizes suddenly increase (e.g., from 1k to 5k), compute needs rise proportionally — suggest a separate ceiling policy to detect distribution shifts and trigger emergency scale.
- If VPC egress cap is hit, the platform should prioritize model response traffic and backpressure client SDKs. We'll provide a snippet of SDK-side retry/backoff guidance.

I attached a quick workbook with the numbers above and a short egress sim. Markus, please add any network-level constraints we should flag. Laura, any procurement-friendly SKU language you want me to include before sending to the customer?

Thanks,
Rishi

Subject: Re: Private deployment questions — sustained bursts and egress caps

Alex — attaching the workbook and short ops checklist (see attachments). TL;DR decision points for Polaris:

1) Reserve an 8-GPU private pool (recommended split: 5 active, 2 warm, 1 spare).
2) Network: dual 25 Gbps NICs (bonded) if you can; at minimum request transient egress allowance to 1 Gbps during warmup windows.
3) Ops controls: soft admission at 70% utilization, hard failover to hosted at sustained 90% (2 minutes).

Next steps:
- Can you share a brief token-size histogram for a typical 20-minute window? That will let us tighten the estimate and possibly move from 8 -> 6 GPUs if outputs are at the lower end.
- If you want the procurement wording, we can include an optional warm-pool SKU that gives you 2 pre-warmed instances billed at a reduced standby rate.

Attachments: throughput_model_v1.xlsx, network-egress-sim.pdf, privgpu-ops-checklist.md

Happy to set a 30-minute call this week to walk through the workbook with your infra team.
